Dear Salt Lake County Council, I watched the meeting you held last night online. I appreciate the civility with which you all conducted yourselves. I am writing to ask you to uphold the 30 day mask mandate. Those who do not wish to follow it in schools have the option to opt out. I have children at Taylorsville high school and Bennion junior high. They have worn masks at school all year and have been completely fine with wearing them. They often forget to take their masks off when they come home. Just in this last week we have received 3 notices of exposure at school. The Covid numbers have exploded. Our hospitals are once again reaching the status of being overwhelmed. Last week, my neighbor's grandfather had to shop around to find a hospital that would take him while he was in need of emergency care for a life threatening situation. This should not be a political matter. A 30 day mask mandate will increase mask wearing, for that short time, decrease the explosion of cases, and show our health care workers that we care about them and that we also care about all those who will need treatment in hospitals over the coming weeks. Hospital surges tend to come roughly 2 weeks after case surges, so we haven't yet seen how overwhelmed the hospitals will become from the current surge. Masking for 30 days is a tiny sacrifice that will make a huge impact, not immediately, but with time, as we see the numbers decrease and the hospitalizations decrease. Please do not overturn this mandate. My children feel safe in school with the mandate. They are hoping to be able to continue to attend in person, to have concerts, to have plays, to go on school tours. They have lost so much the last two years. Wearing masks when the need is there gives them the opportunity to have these wonderful experiences. It was a timely and necessary mandate. -- -Rebekah Pitts

subject: Mask mandate
comment: Councilman Wharton, Overall I think you all have been doing a great job, but please don't let us revert back to a mask mandate driven mindset. I own multiple restaurants in six different states across the country and the way we have responded to the covid virus over the last year or two has allowed our restaurants here in Utah to be the best performing in the chain. We cannot revert back to overreactive and counterproductive measures (i.e. mask mandates) that hinder the social and communicative growth of our kids in school and the increased madness and negativity/depression that a new mask mandate will bring to our communities. We need to accept the fact that, just like the traditional cold and flu, covid is not going away and we cannot continue to upend our lives and live in a constant state of paranoia every time cases get too high. We need to stop openly publishing daily covid cases and focus on treating the elderly and those that actually need help, very similarly to how we have done during traditional cold/flu seasons. Please overturn the mask mandate, and instead continue to emphasize the use of masks and vaccinations. We need to move forward, not backward. Thank you for your consideration and continued efforts. Hello, As a manager at a store in the Gateway mall, I have gotten very used to the homeless situation down in this area. I have been punched by them, yelled at by them on a daily basis, and I have our mall's security on speed dial so I can receive back up when dealing with homeless people at my store. More and more I am becoming a babysitter where I have to watch them come in and steal things. Depending on the size of them determines if I confront them or not. I am not about to go up against anybody on drugs who is bigger than me. Unfortunately the mall security really can't do much except kick them out after they've continuously stolen from us. And then they just disappear onto 500 W where they can't be touched by the security. And then they come back the next day, only to have the same situation happen. I live right above the Gateway mall at 55 S 500 W at the Altitude on Fifth. Despite our new locks on the front doors, I have run into a lot of homeless people in our apartment. Just this week I caught a homeless woman on drugs looking into my patio and my neighbors patios. After talking to my neighbor, my neighbor told me that she had caught her on camera going through her trash and had seen her hiding in the stairways. But, unfortunately the security can only kick them out and then the homeless find their way back in only hours later. Last night, not only did I see the same woman at my work, who I promptly kicked out, but then she was in the stairway again. Not only that, there was another homeless person sleeping on patios by our fire escape. If the homeless can't get in through the front door, I have seen them roll under the garage gate into the garage below. I have had my car broken into and I know quite a few people who have also had their cars broken into. I understand that this isn't an easy fix. But it's getting to the point where my neighbors and I are going to start calling the police - which I think they have bigger fish to fry than deal with homeless junkies who are trespassing and causing havoc at local businesses. We really don't want to call the police if we don't have to because they have other things they should be doing. But it's getting really bad here at the Gateway, and unfortunately we don't have the resources to do much to maintain our safety. I've told my coworkers to have the mall security walk them home if they need it, I never walk alone by myself here at night, and I always carry pepper spray throughout my apartment complex just in case I run into anyone who doesn't live here. It's very unsettling to have my patio and my apartment be open to anybody who can walk up. I will be passing along your email address to my neighbors and a few fellow business owners as we all have had our own accounts with the homeless and are getting to our wit's end.

Dear Councilmember Valdemoros, My name is Michael Mejia and I serve on the Salt Lake Art + Design Board for District 4. I am writing you today to ask for your support of the Arts Council s request for additional staff positions in Budget Amendment 6. I understand that many Departments within Salt Lake City are struggling with needs for staffing support, and you have many staffing requests in this budget amendment for consideration. It is a challenging position to be in and I appreciate your consideration and service to our community. * Many of the Arts Council s programs have grown over the last few years including the creation of the Living Legacy Video Series and Finch Lane Flash Projects, maintenance responsibilities for the newly passed percent for art ordinance, new City Arts Grants categories, and an ever increasing volume of requests and grants, participation in multiple City stakeholder and advisory groups and initiatives such as Fleet Block and Gentrification Mitigation, and increased efforts with equity, inclusion, and community outreach. RE: SALT LAKE CITY COUNCIL AGENDA, March 22, 2022 C. POTENTIAL ACTION ITEMS. 1. Ordinance: Amendment to Require Notice for Permits to Work in the Public Way Dear Councilmember Fowler, Salt Lake City residents have requested notification for work being done in the Right of Way. Citizens express wanting more transparent, accurate information about construction work that can be seen out the window of their house or that affect parking on the street near their home. Verizon supports these goals, but requests the City Council take additional input rather than adopting the ordinance in its current form. In order to address the needs described above, the information must be timely, correct and useful. Verizon notes several concerns with the proposed ordinance: * Operational Challenges - Verizon's construction scheduling process. The current draft of the proposed ordinance to require notification of construction in the right of way may not meet these criteria. Adoption of a quality ordinance cannot be rushed, a few weeks of additional insight and discussion could result in a more seamless adoption and implementation by City Staff and an accurate, timely notice for residents for years to come. We encourage the City Council to take time to consider the language and processes that will provide SLC citizens with well-timed, clear, accurate information about upcoming construction in the ROW. The current draft of the ordinance may benefit from more consideration of the timing, description of the residents who receive notice, the types of proof of notification required, and from further City Staff input. Below is a summary of considerations for the City Council to determine if the proposed ordinance can be improved: 1. Notice period too long - We encourage more time for the City Council where we can discuss further these issues. To be clear, Verizon does not object to providing notification of construction in the right-of way. As a matter of fact, Verizon already voluntarily provides construction notification. Rather, Verizon seeks to assist in optimal regulation that are beneficial to its residents, regulated industry and the City. CONSIDERATIONS FOR SALT LAKE CITY'S PROPOSED NOTICE ORDINANCE - The ordinance is proposed to broadly apply to all ROW users. This presents challenges given the various occurrences of the ROW, how they use it, how they are regulated, and how they perform their installations (timeframe, method, etc.). - As a wireless carrier, Verizon Wireless notes two primary areas that present challenges for the City, the public, and wireless carriers: 1. Notice provided too late to allow for advance planning - such as not two weeks for customers) - especially if the ROW needs to be cleared for construction. - Pre-application notification may give recipients the impression that there is more ability for public input on the location of wireless facilities than is provided for under federal law. - Not all applications are ultimately permitted and constructed. * Fatigue - The City has noted that constituents feel construction fatigue. If broad construction time frames or notice of sites that are not ultimately constructed are provided, this could increase, not reduce, construction complaints from residents who are fatigued by what they thought they would be served by. * Public feedback - The notice is broadly extensive and will lead to confusion by notifying owners of properties that are adjacent to ROW property that will not be affected. While the notice is limited to "Adjacent Properties", the definition of properties and geographic areas may not be clear if impacted properties are adjacent to the above ground work site or to underground facilities being placed from the work site. Sincerely, Kudel Jakubczak Director - Government and Community Affairs Utah, Nevada & Tribal Nations

Dear Ms Fowler: I hope that you will consider making changes to the current rules around Auxiliary Dwelling Units. It's time to examine the current roadblocks that are standing in the way of homeowners like me who would like to add an appropriate ADU to their property. I began making plans to build a 2-car garage with an ADU above it a few years ago, and ran into two main difficulties. The first is that the current rule only allows an ADU to be 50% of the square footage of the original structure. This probably seems reasonable in the abstract, but I live on .16 of an acre, and my home is 768 square feet. That leaves ample room on my property for an additional structure while leaving plenty of yard space. However, a 384 square foot ADU is just too small. Secondly, the rules require a very large buffer around the property line, which would result in the garage/ADU taking over the center of my back yard. I can understand that there could be some concerns about an ADU being built right next to a neighbor's home. However, the current rule seems extreme. In addition, I have alleys on the side and back of my property, so there would not be any impact on neighbors even if it were built next to the property line. Given these circumstances, I emailed the city to learn how to request a review to see if I could be granted an exemption or waiver. I was informed that there was no process to appeal regardless of the circumstances I described. I put my dreams on hold until a chance encounter with Mayor Mendenhall this past summer reignited my plans. I explained to her the challenges I had experienced, and she assured me that I shouldn't have any problem with my plans given my circumstances. She thought that the rule was that an ADU could be 650 square feet or 50% of the original structure size. She also assured me that there was a way to appeal the proximity to the property line given the alleys. Game changer! As reasonable as the 650 square foot rule sounds, it is not how the rule currently reads. I tell you this story not to throw the Mayor under the bus (it's not reasonable to expect her to know every rule), but because the current rule is so limited even our leaders can't believe it's the current reality! I hope that in addition to looking at the size limit and proximity to the property line issues you will also look at height limitations. I hadn't given it any thought since I have 2 story houses around mine, but I understand that the height limitation rules also create issues for those interested in adding an ADU above a garage. As you look for solutions to the housing challenges that Salt Lake is facing, I hope that you will adjust the ADU rules so that homeowners like me can be part of the solution. Thank you for your time and consideration. Jennifer Mabey

I am trying to not conflate the actions of those governing to some sort of greed, but I am struggling. With that being said, in areas that have historically had insufficient off-street parking (like unauthorized parking in the lots of near by businesses), with the associated issues of providing for adequate snow removal, street cleaning, and access for emergency vehicles. Do you really want to drive away those of us with the means to move away from the results of such zoning and regulation changes?

I live in the Guadalupe neighborhood. It's a small neighborhood sandwiched by I-15 to the west and the railroad to the east. To my dismay, half of this small neighborhood is labeled TSA (TSA-T, TSA-U). If notice the city has changed the descriptions of these zones—they used to be TSA-core, TSA-transitional, etc.) The other half of my neighborhood is residential (SR-1A, SR-3). The TSA zone in the neighborhood is already filled with high density apartment buildings mostly for the University of Utah students. We also have a Planned Urban Development, which also owns an event center, the Union, in our small neighborhood. And we have at least one more development, Koto House, coming. Our streets are packed with cars from these new developments. When there is a concert at the Union, our neighborhood streets turn into a parking lot for the event center. If I didn't have a garage, I would have to park a few miles away and walk home. Looking at the proposed document, I am not sure if the city is joking or serious. No minimum off-street parking in TSA-U?! No minimum off-street parking for studios in TSA-T?! That is a developer's heaven and the residents' hell. Doesn't the city understand that the people who live in the TSA zone are parking in the residential zones? Why can't the city get rid of the requirement for parking permits to get rid of off-street parking and put the burden on us, who live in the residential zones? I have one serious solution to offer: give all the residents in Guadalupe neighborhood stickers that say "TSA," "TSA guest," "SR," and "SR guest" depending on their addresses free of charge. And put up parking signs on the street that say "TSA" and "SR only." It's just like college parking lots. We should park within our "zone." If not, we will be ticketed. Concert goers will have to take public transportation because there wont be any parking in the neighborhood for non-sticker holders. This way the city will get more revenues from parking violations, and the residents in the residential zones don't have to worry about carrying their groceries for a mile.

Be careful on modifying off street parking requirements already too few parking spots in many of our high density housing areas. Way too much high density housing development already. We need a pause in SLC to see what residents are most concerned about the rampant growth in SLC making our city a less desirable place to live.

I received a flyer in today's mail inviting input on the upcoming public hearing on Affordable Housing Incentive Proposal. None of the websites listed on the flyer would connect when I tried to access them, so I am writing to the Council. The non-working websites is indicative of Salt Lake City government - much of it doesn't work and doesn't usually represent the citizens desires. As 58 year residents, We strongly oppose the proposed zone changes specifically allowing incentives to the following: Affordable single family detached housing, townhouses. Each of these proposals will increase the number of residents and impact the already crowded streets for driving and parking. Under the current parking ordinance our city streets allow parking on both sides of the street which does not allow for two lanes of vehicular travel. One vehicle has no find an open spot and pull over so the vehicle traveling in the opposite direction can pass. It also presents a safety issue when children are present either playing or walking to and from the nearby schools. Moreover we bought our home in a single family resident area and if the proposed shared housing ordinance is passed we sell move from Salt Lake City, as many of our neighbors have said they would. Sincerely, Richard Moffat

We support an increase in affordable housing, but are opposed to these structures being placed surreptitiously in the middle of neighborhoods (particularly SugarHouse) where traffic is becoming increasingly dense and parking more difficult. There are many areas of the city, particularly near downtown, that are unoccupied and essentially rotting. These areas should be revitalized and could be good locations for affordable housing. Focusing on areas that are already developed and struggling to manage high volumes of traffic, parking issues, and/unnecessary large vehicles, will only make matters worse. Specifically, the Sugarhouse area is bursting at the seams with multiple vehicles for each dwelling. Placing high density housing in these areas would take advantage of areas within our City that need serious redevelopment and could be utilized to house lower income individuals as well as the remaining continued rising population. Thank you.

I don't want fit for four plexes in my neighborhood. Wehave narrow streets and parking gets crowded already on the side streets. I don't want the over crowding, big buildings belong in the business districts or new areas. DOn't destroy our quiet peaceful neighborhood. I was an apt manager for 10 years. This Sugar House area CANNOT continue to withstand ANY more exponential growth as it has the last several years! More building along with on street parking Only benefits the developers, certainly not the long term residents. This IS making this area UN-Livable! I want to be sensitive to the housing needs but not to the Continued detriment of the current residents. So PLEASE NO FURTHER DEVELOPMENTS and/or on street parking.

There are cars parked illegally all the time, because they don't want to trek for three miles to their apartment. It is irresponsible to keep building these giant complexes and not include enough parking. It is awful for everyone in those buildings and everyone in the area. While the reduction in required off-street parking for TSA zones may have seemed like a good idea. In practice, and especially in certain locations (for example, the Guadaloupe neighborhood: 500 W to I-15, North Temple to 600 N), it creates more problems than it solves. Not requiring high-density housing projects to provide sufficient parking for their residents means that public streets are regularly filled to over-flowing. This results in a very unfair allocation of available on-street parking for SR1 and SR2 residents. Please reconsider the parking requirements in areas where TSA and SR zones adjoin. Thank you.

Hello Dan, I hope all your projects are going well. I have spent the last 6 weeks or so hoping to play tennis at Highland high. In the beginning we found the courts to be open, but in the last four weeks they have been locked. I have traveled to two other high school s in the area and both of them have had their courts open. What compelled me to write today is what I experienced today. Today is an asynchronous day. I went to play at 10am – the courts were occupied – OK it is tennis season – some leeway needs to be recognized. I went back at about noon and the courts were locked – that is not acceptable. The highland high tennis courts are not the private tennis club for the highland high coach. Due to her own actions I would like to see action from the city to remedy this problem. The courts should be available to the public, and they should not be locked. After the season ends they should not be excessively occupied by the tennis coach, or prioritized by the Highland high tennis team. They should be on a first come first serve basis as is the case with all other public courts. The tennis teacher can throw out a lot of excuses such as the courts are wet due to dripping water, and we are protecting the courts, or we are in the middle of the season. If a person gets hurt climbing the fence, that could lead to some serious repercussions for the city. This needs to be addressed. Please let me know. Daniel

Requiring fewer parking stalls could lower the cost of new development, including housing; but fewer off-street parking stalls could increase parking challenges in some neighborhoods." The current street parking congestion make those things a challenge for current residents. Additional street parking will make the parking congestion unmanagable.

Reducing the number of off street parking stalls for new developments can help provide more units, 1-bed to 2-bed is more based on the population to be housed in multi-family development and good access to public transit is crucial. We can't have developments like this in neighborhoods which are already overwhelmed with on street parking but if done well, this can be some helpful.

I am against the proposal to require fewer off-street parking stalls in new developments. I lived in Salt Lake for over 40 years as a Salt Lake City resident, and I've seen who's hurt the most vulnerable. Although reducing this requirement might attract more developers, it passes the burden on to those who live in and use these spaces. I lived in low-income housing in the downtown area and we were often forced to park blocks from our home (with two small children) or pay for parking, which was hard on an already strained budget. Additionally, multi-family structures like 5-over-1s are already notorious for attracting developers who cut costs with substantial materials. We need more affordable housing, but we should have more strict building regulations, not more permissive regulations, if we want people to ACTUALLY be able to live and thrive in our community.

topic: Proposed Changes to RMF-30 Zoning District
comment: I received a housing pamphlet from the city council and just wanted to share my feedback. I believe the changes to the RMF 30 zoning is a good idea. topic: Proposed Changes to RMF-30 Zoning District
comment: Hello! I just got the mailer from city council about the various initiatives in the works on affordable housing, including shared housing, RMF-30 Zoning, and changes to off-street parking. I am encouraged by these changes and I support all of them. Specifically, regarding the zone changes, we need to get creative in providing affordable housing options. I know many in my Rose Park neighborhood bemoan changes that would make it "the next Sugar House," but I think the only way to prevent the displacement of families and to provide long-term opportunities for diverse citizens, families, immigrants, and more, is to provide a variety of housing options. The single family home only zoning increases housing costs, causes more pollution from long commutes, and creates barriers to home ownership for many sometimes. Also, we don't have to become the Sugar House with this change. It could be something in between! I know the last public hearing already happened, but I am curious about this direction.

I have a driveway I share with five other families - it exits onto 800 south which has become increasingly busy over the years. My concern continues to be that residents park on 800 south immediately adjacent to the exit of the driveway. This significantly impacts those exiting the driveway ability to see cyclists and approaching cars as we exit. Despite multiple calls to the city this continues to not be unresolved. I am terrified that somebody I am going to hit someone. All that would be needed to resolve this is a parking buffer for a few feet so that drivers exiting the driveway have a view of 800 South that is not obstructed.
Sounds like a reasonable housing situation, however, it also may need to have a "house parent" on sight to oversee that the shared areas are respected by all.

As stated in the proposal, requiring fewer parking stalls by the developer will result in tenants parking on side streets. This is already an issue due to the number of rental units in my area - particularly with the number of next registered AirBnBs. An arrangement for homeowners needs to be made.

Hello SLC Council, We need to ban private companies owning more than x single family homes in the city. That is hard to define and tracking but it is a cause worth prioritizing is having a huge impact on young people and lower income people. Citizens who could once afford homes and start building real wealth are being priced out. Please, do something. I received your mailer about affordable living incentives and shared housing. Yes those things can help but we need more wholesale changes to go along with these smaller impact items. I am aware the majority of the state legislature are realtors and land developers. Let's show other states that even though there is an appearance of conflict of interest on housing matters related matters, here in Utah we are not corrupt and we give everyone a fair shake. Take bigger action than what you have planned, please. Sincerely, Michael Heath Rose Park

I want to THANK YOU for your support with regard to the integrity of the Salt Lake City foothill trails. I hope that you follow the recommendations of the Salt Lake City Public Lands and was permission to: Extend the pause on trail construction until spring 2023 Release funds to restore and re-vegetate the Avenues Ridgeline Trail above Terrace Hills trailhead Release funds to allow for maintenance and repair of original "legacy" and recently constructed trails with the use of hand tools only Expand the scope of work for a review and assessment of the 2020 Foothills Trails System Plan and work done during Phase 1 Release funds to allow the study and design for the new trailheads I am a frequent user (along with my wife and family) of the foothill trails especially those in the Terrace Hills/Twin Peaks area. We are hikers and birders. This past year I have enjoyed viewing two juvenile eagles that soar over the foothills from their nests. Over the years I have watched mountain bikers and hikers as they walk through and scarred the foothills and left miles of erosive new trail cuts. I totally agree with the permissions as stated above and feel that they will serve to improve the quality of the foothill trail system as well as the user experience. Please, let's not make our foothills into a maze of unsightly trail cuts and erosional scars, let's strive to keep the uniqueness of the foothills for all to enjoy. Thanks again. Sincerely, Jim Brandi Salt Lake City

I recently got a letter in the mail about the shared housing proposal and believed that I deserved to have say in it if it goes through or not. I highly don't believe this is a good idea because our city is too crowded enough and we have much worse problems like roads, illegal immigration, trying to make schools without propaganda of any way politically, and soaring water for the people that are already here. The answer to the problem of increasing housing cost for the people here is to get rid of the people that come here to commit petty crime, and crime farther out to other places in the city, and overcrowds the city more than we need. I wanted to email in support of the affordable housing initiatives under consideration by the city council. I am working on my master's degree in public policy and I have done several projects on housing policy. With a few classmates, I wrote the following: https://medium.com/p/14d41264321 Allowing shared housing is a good idea. Reducing parking requirements is a great idea. I think you should eliminate parking minimums, and let developers decide how much parking to build. (I would go so far as to say there should be parking maximums, and fees on surface parking lots to encourage more development). Any changes to zoning laws that allow more density are positive steps and I support these moves fully. I imagine you will get angry opposition from some, but SLC residents understand the need for affordable housing, so these steps are the right steps to take.

Hi, I am opposed to changing zoning allowing single-family homes to smaller apartment buildings. This is a horrible idea. Who would want their neighbors home to be turned into an apartment building?! Please put a quick end to this dumb idea and preserve our beautiful neighborhoods!

Hi folks at SLC Council, Thank you for finally coming to this conclusion, it should have been done 30 years ago, though better late than never. I suggest and highly recommend that the council also provides tiny house and RV housing, but also all sorts of other "adaptable housing options as well, especially for the homeless and low income folk. Thank you for your consideration. Saed Sadeghi.

I support allowing shared housing throughout all of Salt Lake! Shared housing is inherently more affordable than single family and most of other multi-family units. Removing SRO's has created the housing shortage, especially around the Wasatch Front as the state grows. Those who oppose SRO's "in this particular setting" or "in this neighborhood" are selfishly preventing people from being housed. Utah used to be the leader nationwide in the housing-first model for reducing homeless; by allowing more housing of all kinds, we could be leaders again.

The fact that you are even considering to decrease the number of off street parking required for new residences is completely crazy! Already we are finding street parking to be extremely limited in many of the neighborhoods that are being built and re-developed neighborhoods. All the streets are so inundated with parked vehicles to the point currently that they have become one way only streets and you want to add more. I understand that multiple housing projects are necessary and allow for individuals to buy or rent during a housing crisis. But it is being done in a way that is ruining the neighborhoods. Even if you assume that each household has only one vehicle, when the reality is probably two or three, letting any household go without with less than one off-street parking stall per household is short-sighted. The fact that you are even considering reducing the current requirement, which is already inadequate, is the attitude that is causing the existing residents and homeowners to despise the new housing construction coming to their new developments and to complain. Please reconsider.

SLC's roads are in atrocious shape. And they're steadily getting worse. Having too bounce around in a lane is bad and makes cars look unrideable to cyclists and pedestrians, much less other cars. Having reviewed the redistricting maps, it would seem keeping things close to current seems the best for the Sugarhouse community. topic: Proposed Changes to RMF-30 Zoning District
comment: The proposed changes for RMF-30 Zoning is a very bad idea for the city and especially its citizens. I'm a 30 year resident of Salt Lake (in the same house) and have seen many changes in the city. I'm very concerned that these proposed changes will have a lasting and irreversible damages to our neighborhoods. I understand increased density in Salt Lake. 400 South (with units like the Meridian) was designed for high density living and works well. Small lots and multi- family housing (up to 3 or more units - are you kidding me!) will destroy the communities that surround these dense areas. I've seen the damage first hand when the city decided to allow the zoning conversion of single family dwelling units to duplexes if the owner could provide evidence that the unit was rented (illegally by the way) consistently. I still don't understand rewarding individuals for breaking the law but with this change came more cars, parking issues, unmaintained properties, and a transient population that is not invested in our community. It's our communities that make Salt Lake a safe and desirable location. I also don't see any consideration for the spillover effect these zoning changes have onto streets and neighborhoods. It will be devastating to the neighborhoods. Based on the council meeting it seems that many of these housing proposals are meant to benefit developers instead of Salt Lake City citizens and residents. It is your duty to protect our citizens, residents, communities and neighborhoods instead of those who aim to profit from these zoning changes and are not invested in our communities long-term.

By not requiring new apartment construction to require all tenants to pay for a parking stall and building one stall/per unit, tenants tend to use street parking in residential areas, thus depriving homeowners/taxpayers of using the street parking for guest parking. If a tenant doesn't have a car, then they can possibly rent out their stall to someone who needs to have two stalls. The planning commission has made a mess of Sugar House by failing to control off street parking, which has also harmed businesses in the area. Also, some of the proposed street designs also infringes on the rights of homeowners to use street parking by giving way to bikelanes. This is especially true on 1100 East and Highland Dr, where there should never be bike lanes as it is too congested and dangerous. 900 East has suitable bikelanes for bikers to use safely. Not every street needs bike lanes, particularly in the long winter months (when there is snow accumulation). Designers need to become more sensible and sensitive!

It would be great to keep cohesive neighborhoods together since communities like mine function as a unit. If splits could be made where there are major roads rather than smaller neighborhood streets, that would be helpful.

Created to encourage development in the Central 9th area, FB-UN2 was successful in facilitating some great projects and infill development. The community and Central City successfully worked with the Council several years ago to introduce certain minor text amendments to FB-UN2 that improved certain aspects of the zone in situations where it is applied in neighborhoods not zoned entirely under the FB-UN1/FB-UN2 paradigm, but this was never intended fix to greater problems in terms of the realized development we are seeing under FB-UN2 in our City. As you are set to vote this coming week on the rezone of a very large 2.3 acre parcel in the Central City Historic District, I hope that you are aware of the paucity of zoning being experienced by affected constituents regarding this particular zone, which was mentioned in its original design. topic: Proposed Changes to RMF-30 Zoning District
comment: Dear City Council Members, I am contacting you today about concerns I have with the proposed rezone of the property at 1902 South 400 East. The proposal for 1902 South 400 East is requesting a building height of 30-35 Ft. on a lot this size will feel imposing and does not fit the space. The change in setback, in particular, means that a new project zoned at R35 cannot be compared to an older R35 zoned property. The lack of setback completely changes the height perception and presence in the neighborhood. Additionally, I see the following issues: 1 – Lack of setback creates a visibility issue for traffic in the middle of a neighborhood. The new apartments at the corner of 2100 S and 400 E are a great example of how this causes problems for traffic and increases the risk for pedestrians and cyclists. 2 – Increased hardscape in a city increases noise pollution. This is true for a single-family dwelling, but even more so for a higher-density dwelling. 3 – Decreased green space heats up our city, can negatively impact health and well-being, and the state and city have mandatory requirements for temperature regulation. A decrease in green space also increases noise pollution, which is detrimental to residents' health and well-being. There is a wonderful development on 300 E and Ramona that is a great example of how an apartment complex can fit in a neighborhood. It includes green space – primarily water-wise trees and bushes – and the apartments are secluded and set back from the sidewalk. There are methods to moderately increase housing while still being true to the characteristics and suitability of a neighborhood. This proposal is not one of those methods. Thank you for your consideration.

topic: Proposed Changes to RMF-30 Zoning District
comment: Hello Salt Lake City Council, Please review and consider my following concerns/comments regarding the proposed zoning map amendment for the property located at 1902 South 400 East. • Building height of 30-35 Ft. on a lot this size will feel imposing and does not fit the character of the neighborhood • Building setback Using St. Josephs Villa as a reference to what already exists in the neighborhood is misleading. St. Josephs Villas required structure setback relative to building height requirements allow for more green space with less of an imposing structure. The proposed zoning changes allow for a structure that can be considered unattainable due to building height relative to lot size, resulting in an imposing, out of place structure. • Pushing structures to the edge of sidewalks. This has recently happened at new housing at 400 E. 2100 S. Results in dangerous intersections where motorists/cyclists sight lines are diminished, resulting in automobiles needing to enter intersections to see oncoming traffic. • Greenspace makes our city a much more livable place to be. Lack of greenspace results in higher city temperatures. I am not necessarily promoting the use of water consuming turf or plant matter. I am promoting the use of naturally weather tested to survive. High coverage relative to lot size, combined with the use of xeriscaping/drought tolerant plants/green roofing. • Maintaining a building height and setback of shorter apartment buildings in the immediate area would better accommodate the character of the neighborhood. Thank you for your consideration. Shawn Porter

Dear Council Chair Dugan, I am writing to inform you Fairpark Community Council voted in its last general meeting to support the redistricting map labeled as "Politely Compact with Minimal Changes Map." Several reasons informed this decision. First, our easternmost neighbors who live in District 3 want to remain in District 3. They feel the needs of our community are different and frankly have better resources for their issues. Second, we are fearful the last census undercounted the total population of our neighborhood and surrounding communities. Having three representatives as we've had for the last decade will help mitigate this fear. Finally, we are very aware of the new, dense buildings coming online now and in the coming years that will increase the population of our community outside of the redistricting threshold. Given they overlap all three of Fairpark's council districts, we believe keeping the current district alignment is in the best interest of our community and of equitable distribution of representation. Finally, we read an opinion piece in the Salt Lake Tribune on April 21, 2022 calling for support of the map RD2022-04 specifically because of the potential of electing people from historically marginalized communities. This is not what Fairpark neighbors what we wanted. This letter tells you what we want; to remain with three representatives. We hope, you will consider this information as you deliberate in the May 3 work session and in upcoming public meetings. Thank you for your attention. Best regards, Nigel Swaby Chair, Fairpark Community Council

The number one issue facing Salt Lake City - and each of us - is climate change and its disproportionate affects on our planet (humans and non-humans alike). subject: Proposed Changes to RMF-30 Zoning District
topic: RMF-30 Zoning and Related Development Issues in Salt Lake City
comment: Thank you for the recent mailings reaching out to Salt Lake City residents regarding local housing issues and the resulting to the revised zoning requirements. I am responding to the recent amendment to the city's proposed residential zoning outlined in the 24 July 2019 Staff Report and amended 25 September 2019 report. While I agree in principle with the amendments/effects I am against the proposed changes as the unintended consequences of these revisions will unnecessarily concentrate affordable housing in areas that also need improvements within current communities, infrastructure, and employment. Local Historic Districts, and more specifically to the Central City area from 400 South to Liberty Park between 500 and 700 East, I believe this is a prime example of what remains of a quintessential historic Salt Lake City residential neighborhood that is in need of preservation. Much of what has built in that area is in the 1800s and early 1900s. After the subdivision based on the southwestern edge of Liberty Park. Considering the intense development that has taken place in downtown, the largest destruction of historical structures, loss of green space, and the huge, haphazard apartment complexes already built around what used to be a low rise residential area. I support that from many concerned residents an effort to limit the rampant growth that has taken place. The Planning Commission and City Council need to take a step back from about 5-year plans and look 20 to 50 years into the future to try and understand what this type of development will have on the well being of the city. A recent survey by the U of U study and the Kem Gardner Institute released in February 2021 and titled "What do residents think?" contains and itemizes both residents surveyed throughout the city felt that it is necessary to maximize profit, without regard to community and adjacent property impacts. Each development should be considered on a case-by-case basis with input from the Historic Landmark Commission, neighboring property owners, local businesses, and other relevant groups. I think everyone would agree that most residents would like improvements for loss of parking strips and reduced open space to a bare minimum, in the area mentioned above the historic residences have maintained large yards, mature trees in the lots as well as the parking strips and center medians and will continue to do so if they are allowed. Historic zoning protection should be, but hasn't been applied to maintain the high standard of quality in the region. With the large number of new apartments complexes along 400 South and in this Liberty Park vicinity, plus the ones about to presume "walkability" undermining the historical integrity and lived organization isn't such as those from trolley systems, the quality of life has already been compromised. Looking to the future with so many new and large multi unit apartment for the park and nearby businesses. Destruction of historical structures. Despite the included incentives for developers to construct affordable housing structures into new development is a highly unlikely this will happen. The options developers have from on-site affordable housing to-off site construction, and in lieu fee are designed to make a profit that allow and not the result of providing affordable housing that is desperately needed. As a city planning consultant, I find this level of ownership. Everywhere you look in this city, beautiful, viable historic structures have been demolished in the name of expediency, profitability and tax base. Historical structures tell what provide a city with character and, more important, lasting value.

subject: Proposed Changes to RMF-30 Zoning District
topic: RMF-30 Zoning and Related Development Issues in Salt Lake City
comment: As pointed out in the reviews, set unit parking requirements present a very real problem for multi-unit and cottage type developments. The reduction of requirements from two to one space for all street parking will very much impact area residents who are walking to access local facilities, and the "walkability" of the neighborhood. Affordability, as pointed out in the staff reports these zoning changes are not likely to provide substantial affordable units. Rather, these changes are more likely to provide another avenue for developers to take advantage of regulatory changes at the expense of the residents of long-established neighborhoods. Considering the cost of land acquisition and the workplace cost of materials brought on by supply chain issues and demand, developers are categorically unable to provide "affordable housing" again, their objective is to find opportunities and maximize profits. From the perspective of both a resident and a housing advocate, I think we need to realize that historic neighborhood is the most likely alternative with small multi residences and homeowners offering single and multiple family jobs, for rent. If the city wants to preserve the character, and at the same time support affordability, they would do more better to support local people wishing to live in existing structures and provide employment opportunities. I'd like to recommend that the Planning Division Community & Neighborhoods staff, the Planning Commission, the City Council, and Mayor in dealing with a frightening preparation does not mean that identification and zoning of all areas of the city is appropriate Any planners should understand that development is a powerful force that can create both functional and dysfunctional features in a community. Given the history of this city, they will provide a highly desirable real estate market for those young families who move here, live in one of two high apartment complexes, wish to remain and transition to a home that provides a yard in which their children can grow into productive citizens. Those people will likely abandon the community or languish and be unhappy in insufficient housing. Text amendments should not be adopted at this time as Land-anchor change or zoning requirements will adversely open all areas in need of preservation to the long-term destruction and development of existing neighborhoods. However, a number of areas do need increased levels of housing density and these can be addressed through specific zoning changes and design requirements. Ability to construct, side oriented one houses and cottage developments, Limits to maximum lot width, and incentives for retention of historic structures. We not move proposed changes in a project by project basis, while long-term human values and the success of historic elements should be the overriding consideration. This is more important than short-term finance gain.

subject: Dangerous Drivers
comment: I support the neighborhood speed limit from 25 mph to 20 mph on 700 South to address the real problems, namely people driving drunk or impaired by drugs. It seems to me that you made this reduction as a knee-jerk reaction to general fatal accident trends, but such reduction doesn't necessarily address the underlying public and priveleges that you were "doing something." However, in virtually all of these fatal crashes the drivers were drunk or impaired, and it is unlikely that such a small reduction in speed limit will make much of a difference. That said, I believe to something as "trivial" as the speed limit. So clearly the thing to do is to take measures to get those drivers off the streets and to keep them off. Measures such as immediate license revocation and vehicle impoundment upon arrest. And allow no bail penalties for driving without a valid license, proper monitoring of people out on parole or bail, no bail or release for drivers arrested for reckless causing serious injury or fatalities, including immediate notification of parole and probation authorities, and so on. I know much of this is outside to the city council's purview, but you could work with the state legislature and the courts to get stiffer laws. Also, the state could surely enact laws allowing and encouraging the use of speed cameras than that one being wasted on changing speed limit signs. Please don't punish all drivers, most of whom are law abiding and sober, by forcing everyone to drive at horse and buggy speeds. Thank you.

subject: Biker/walker commuter safety
comment: Hi City Council, I recently sold my car and have been relying solely on biking, walking, and public transit to get around Salt Lake City. I'm deeply concerned for biker & walker safety on the streets of Salt Lake, as I've found out as a bike commuter our city is designed for cars, not people or bikes. I recently watched this video that showed Salt Lake's streets through the lens of pedestrian and bicyclist safety. Salt Lake City was used as an example of one of the more dangerous places to be a pedestrian and cross the street. This doesn't make me a proud Salt Lake citizen. Our city is designed for cars, and everytime I'm commuting I do fear for my safety here. I would strongly support adding infrastructure to make biking and walking in Salt Lake City safer, including additional protected bike lanes (not just shoulders) across the city, continuous sidewalks, independent traffic lights, and slowing down drivers. This would provide better options for commuters and reduce our dependency on cars, which will also work to improve Salt Lake's air quality (another issue I'm very concerned about, but warrants it's own comment). For being such an active city I'm surprised by the lack of bike infrastructure, and by designing our roads only for cars we discourage commuters from even trying to commute by bike. I would love for Salt Lake to lead the way by following Amsterdam's example, and designing our city for our people and not their cars.

My wife and I have been aware of and have been following the tremendously successful efforts of The Other Side Academy to help the homeless and those who struggle with chronic problems in their lives. We have donated money and time to them, and feel that the current plan to create a set of tiny homes in Salt Lake City is a tremendously positive endeavor. Salt Lake has struggled with its homeless population that currently exists. It's been a difficult road, and I know that the city has been looking for viable solutions. For a ridiculously small contribution of land (approximately 8000 sq feet), and the Academy contributing $2.5 million in direct investment, the city will be able to pivot to a new approach that hasn't been tried before. We have been to the other side Academy and have seen the incredible change that has happened in the lives of the people who have passed through their program. I am so pleased that you all can now take this important step. We thank you for your efforts, and many, many people will thank you for decades to come. Sincerely, Brad and Gayle Myler Highland, Utah

subject: Support for The Other Side Village Vote
comment: Hello! I am a student at Utah Valley University majoring in Political Science and minoring in Peace and Justice Studies. I first started with The Other Side Village as a volunteer about a year ago then was hired on as the Communications Manager back in February of this year. I wanted to express my support for the Village and the rezoning of the plot that will be used by it. I normally write on behalf of the Village, but for this public comment, I'm writing it myself. There are generally 3 main (and understandable) concerns that appear regarding this planned community: Safety, Crime, and Cleanliness. The Village has addressed all three of these thoroughly and many times. In short, these are the reasons why the Village is a good idea and is deserving of the approval and support that it is asking for: 1. A combination of 200% accountability and extensive support. You know that you hit the sweet spot when you get opposition from both sides of the political spectrum, progressives are concerned that the Village will have too high of accountability/requirements for residents and conservatives are concerned that it will have too low. The reason for this false dichotomy, the Village will perpetuate a culture of 200% accountability (responsible not just for yourself, but for your neighbors as well) AND utilize involved and in-touch support such as basic needs, medical support, therapy, and behavioral coaching from professionals (Valley Behavioral Health), vocational opportunities, social events, and others. The Village believes it is a form of prejudice to decide beforehand what someone can or cannot do, they believe in providing opportunities and empowering people to succeed, not limiting the opportunities available and what they plan to do. 2. Misconceptions It's an unfortunate belief that those experiencing homelessness are often criminals. In reality, they are often the victims of crimes. "Community First!" in Austin Texas is a similar program to the Village and has had multiple crimes reported inside their community that were committed by residents of a nearby neighborhood, and 0 crimes reported outside of the community that were committed by "Community First" residents, turning that misconception on its head. Furthermore, most people that visit the Village remark on how safe they feel there. In reality, property values have only increased. These are powerful anecdotes, especially considering that the Village will be more structured, more therapeutic, and (in my personal opinion) more effective than the "Community First" program.

subject: Support for The Other Side Village Vote

subject: The Other Side Village
comment: Council members I am pleased that you are considering a zone change of the historic landfill site for the Other Side Village. I have been surprised that it has taken a considerable amount of time for you to consider this matter. I am very supportive of the proposal to build roughly 400 homes for those currently living in encampments through the city. Here are the reasons for my affirmative position. The management of the Other Side Academy have addressed homelessness at other locations. Since they began their program in Herriman several years ago, their community began to thrive and the population can learn, change, and more than 70% of their graduates reintegrate positively into society. They have done this without any financial support from government including Salt Lake. This same farm is willing to build a village on another available site in our city. They have already accomplished this with the same principles they have they have used at the Other Side Academy. Principles that help individuals become self-reliant not just warehoused problems. Healthcare will be addressed on premises; families who wish to work will be able to be employed, provide the grounds on and off site. The peer support model used at the Other Side Academy will help insure that the village residents comply with the standards established by the community. The first phase will occupy about 8 acres, as I understand. This will account for roughly 200 homes. If the experiment goes well, they will expand to roughly 200 homes eventually. The Applicant is willing to clean up the cities environmental problems, build all of the improvements, and manage the 8 acre project with no financial help from the city. Why isn't the city saying heck yeah, how fast can you get this built??? Think about this. Even in the very unlikely event that the project doesn't meet the cities expectations and the ground lease is defaulted the city becomes the owner of an affordable housing project worth $8000,000 having paid nothing for it! Doesn't this sound like a great gamble for the city to take? From what I understand the project appears to be successful. Please provide a way for this project to be built and managed by those who have proven they are worthy of your trust. Make it easy not difficult with imposed unnecessary burdens. Let the Other Side Academy build the first phase and prove that it is a good thing for the whole city. If it is as successful as I hope it will be, please expedite the approval of the balance of the site. With Respect

comment: Greetings, I would like to submit my comments in support of your approval for The Other Side Village. We desperately need this housing and I am all in favor of the project. The advantages are numerous, and I believe any negatives can be effectively managed. I agree that it is wise to start with a pilot project then assess what is working well and what needs to be improved, but we should be looking to the future and plan to implement the full project. I first started working with the unsheltered population way back in the late 1980's first as a volunteer and then subsequently have been working with this population for more than 30 years. Over the years I have worked with thousands of people who are unsheltered, and specifically individuals facing addiction and mental illness. I understand very well the challenges in serving these populations. I believe that creating permanent, long term solutions but this project is not the only reasonable way to move forward. Short term solutions like 'camp abatements' and temporary winter overflow shelters are costly and ultimately only marginally effective. Getting people into stable housing is the only way to help them to get off the streets permanently. I know from personal experience that some individuals thrive in the setting like The Other Side and most of all, HOPE that people need to better their lives. I have interacted with the staff and employees of both The Other Side Boutique Thrift Store and The Other Side Movers. I was very impressed by everyone, and I believe that all of these staff who will be working directly with the Village residents are well qualified, well trained, experienced, dedicated or unsheltered. They were all friendly, considerate, hardworking and provided great service. I have the utmost confidence that The Other Side Village will be just as well run and effective in this new mission as they have been with these other programs. This success will save the city money by reducing EMS calls, police calls, hospital visits, camp abatements and other services. I believe that you should approve the lease for the pilot project for the full 40 year term. Our city needs to stop wasting money on band-aid approaches and start investing in real solutions. I trust it will be supported by the city. This will make project fund raising easier, as donors want to know that their money will go to a stable, viable project. It also enables the non-profit to focus on running the pilot program rather than needing to continue to work on receiving city support. PLEASE APPROVE THIS PROJECT!!! Respectfully, Kandy Richards

comment: Dear Salt Lake City Councilmembers, It is my pleasure to submit this letter of support on behalf of The Other Side Village (TOSV). Since it was first announced in 2021, I've had the privilege of meeting repeatedly with TOSV's team. During this process, I've had the opportunity to provide feedback, share concerns, and participate in the planning process for the village. Representatives of TOSV presented to the Glendale Neighborhood Council and Poplar Grove Community Council in September of 2021. During this meeting they repeatedly answered questions from residents and presented their vision for the site. They later hosted a Design Charrette with residents and community leaders, myself included, to solicit feedback from the community and to answer the myriad of questions we had. I'm impressed with how TOSV's team regularly participates in community cleanup activities in Glendale and volunteered as part of our team during NeighborWorks Salt Lake's Take Your Heart Out event. As I have gotten to know TOSV's team and leadership more over the past year, I've been most impressed with their sincere care for our most vulnerable population. I offer my support to this project and encourage you to do so as well. The proposed zoning amendment request, which was approved by the Salt Lake City Planning Commission on October 27, 2021, is an important step forward. I would encourage you to approve a rezone for the entire project rather than only the initial pilot area. The prospects of going through the extended process each time an expansion is begun is daunting and hinders the ability for creation of new structures in a timely and efficient manner. The Other Side Village project will not only provide stable housing but also important gathering space for all members of the community. New amenities like a bodega, sport courts, community performance space, a nondenominational chapel, and green space will revitalize a currently underutilized area and promote a thriving urban neighborhood on the city's Westside. With your support, this vacant land is slated to become an innovative and impactful symbol of our city's commitment to ending homelessness. I'm proud to support this effort to address homelessness alongside providing access to essential resources to help our neighbors get back on their feet and along the Jordan River. I'm writing today to encourage the Salt Lake City Council to support this critical resource for our community. Thank you, Turner C. Bitton (he/him)

subject: SLC needs an affordable housing loss mitigation
comment: Howdy! This is Tim Funk, Crossroads Urban Center forwarding our statement that SLC needs an affordable housing loss mitigation ordinance. We believe the ordinance is necessary before you proceed with adoption of RMF-30, SMD or off-street parking measures. According to Harvard University between 2013 and 2018 over 25,000 affordable housing units in the SLC metro area were demolished or had their price increased beyond what low income renters can afford. During this same period SLC has increased by over 15,000 rental units, but these have been largely unaffordable to working families. SLC loses an affordable unit for every new development. While new development produces some city's diversity, makes it more challenging for employers to find workers and women as qualify by increasing commute times. In addition this situation has worsened over the last two plus years because of increased real estate inflation and the continuing pandemic. The predicament is simplified as developers in SLC are currently not incentivized to preserve affordable housing units nor are penalized when new developments destroy existing affordable housing units. SLC desperately needs our City Council to prioritize an affordable housing loss mitigation ordinance and work together to pass an affordable housing loss ordinance that includes the following three elements: 1) A requirement the developers report to the City not just how many housing units will be destroyed by a project, but, specifically how many naturally-occurring affordable housing units will be destroyed, 2) A requirement that affordable housing units that are destroyed by the new development or pay $100,000 per unit into the city trust fund to help spur the replacement elsewhere, and, 3) A requirement that developers pay $10,000 into a relocation fund for every affordable unit destroyed to help low income tenants displaced by the development to find a new place to live. Such a mitigation ordinance with these three elements should be in place before any officials move forward with any proposals to approve RMF-30, RMU, SMD, or off-street parking measures. We urge you to make affordable housing living in our City. Thank you Crossroads looks forward to working with you in making our city affordable to everyone who lives here now or chooses to in the future. Best regards, Tim Funk

subject: "The Other Side Village"
comment: Dear City Council, I'm writing to urge you to vote in favor of building The Other Side Village. There have been many comments made from concerned neighbors about how this village will affect crime rates in the neighborhood. It's fair that these people are correlating homelessness with an increase in crime; people in desperate situations will take drastic actions that others can't even imagine. However, I'd like to point out that with the construction of The Other Side Village, we will not simply be concentrating homelessness in this one neighborhood. The difference here is that these people will no longer be homeless. The Other Side Village will not only offer these people a safe place to sleep, eat and shower, but it will also offer a community with a social network of support. These people who were once in a desperate situation will finally have their basic needs met and will be able to be contributing members of society. The Other Side Village concept is not simply "another place to put homeless people"; it's a solution to homelessness. Please remember this as you listen to comments from people who don't want a homeless camp in their backyard. No one wants a homeless camp in their backyard. The Other Side Village WILL NOT be a homeless camp. It will be a community of engaged citizens. It will be our first step in ensuring that we do not have homeless camps built in any more backyards. subject: Budget amendment No. 3 from Sept 20, 2022
comment: To City Council, Concerning Budget Amendment No. 3: A one-time $6 million amount to address what you're calling "deeply affordable" housing is not going to actually solve the problem we have. I hope that is understood and I hope no one upon the council is under such a false pretense. This amount of money will not go nearly far enough to actually address and change the issue of homelessness and recurring homelessness in Salt Lake City. The definition of what is considered "affordable" is what needs to be addressed and changed as soon as possible. Currently, it being at 80% AMI is frankly ridiculous, considering the AMI is usually shown to be at least 60k, sometimes exceeding 70k. This is such a load of b.s. because you're taking the exceptionally wealthy people and grouping them in with folks that are making hardly anything, and pretending there is actually some sort of middle ground they can meet in (the median). To truly meet the needs in terms of affordability in rent, you must reduce what is considered "affordable" in your definitions and policies from 80% down to 30%. The council and this year's budget, the way it is written, is incentivizing landlords and developers, both predatory professions by nature, for essentially not doing anything, except accepting slightly less money for owning property. There is nothing in the incentive program that demands that landlords/developers must make necessary improvements to properties, nor is there anything about required maintenance. And there should be! It is shameful on them, and the City Council, for not doing more to address inequities in this City, especially when some have so much, and many have so little. Please do take and use the $6 million, but get back to public meetings, public hearings, and discuss how you will get "affordability" on track to reflect what is actually affordable for most people in need, and not just make it about any given area's "median income". Or if you're going to keep it that way, using median income, define "affordable" as 30% AMI instead of 80% AMI. Thank you. -James Miska

subject: The Other Side Village
comment: Dear City Council, The summer before I moved to Salt Lake City, my friends and I were discussing my upcoming move across the country. "Did you know they actually solved homelessness in Salt Lake City?", one friend asked. "Yea, I heard about that. The actually use Housing First policies there," another friend agreed. I was ecstatic to move to a city that actually made big steps towards providing housing to our most vulnerable neighbors. Now 6 years later, I am reminded everyday how misled my friends were. I am reminded everyday that I live in a city that is too scared and too inert to do anything towards this problem. Where I live, when I look out my window, the people I usually see are transient folks hanging out on the park strip across the road from my house. A few years ago, during one cold stretch in the dead of winter, a young man lived under a pile of blankets and would wait for hours at a time at night, right outside my kitchen window. As a citizen of this city, this hard on me. I don't like living in a city where my neighbors' basic needs aren't being met. I want to live in the city my friends told me Salt Lake was. I am very excited to hear about The Other Side Village. I think this model is very aligned with the Housing First ideal I put a lot of hope in; the concept that led my friends to think that Salt Lake had solved homelessness. I think a community of modest, affordable housing and strong social supports is a great first step in undoing this mess of homelessness we have here in this city. I strongly believe that homelessness is not indicative of the flaws of the individuals affected but instead it is indicative of the flaws of the city that allows it. I ask you to vote in favor of buildingThe Other Side Village. Thank you.

It's close to impossible to get and keep a job. With a housing first solution like this tiny home village, we can give some of these people the opportunity to regain financial and social power. I love that this village will provide a strong social network for its occupants. I don't like living in a city that is covered in homeless camps-not because it's an eye sore or because the people both me, but because I don't like what it indicates about the people who live in this city who DO have the power to change things. When I see these camps, or when I see my transient neighbors hanging out across the street, I'm reminded that I live in a city that is unwilling to question and stand up against the status quo. This is not the city I want to live in. Is this the city you want to live in? Thank you. Again, please vote in favor of The Other Side Village.

subject: The Other Side Village

Once a person loses housing, they are at risk for a number of problems. If we want our city to grow sustainably and be economically strong in the future, we must act now and work towards real solutions for affordable housing for everybody. I think that a lot of people see helping the homeless as a charitable act, done out of the goodness of their heart. I see it differently. subject: The Other Side Village
comment: Dear City Council, I'm writing to ask you to vote in favor of the Other Side Village. I would like to point out that this establishment is markedly different from "just another homeless shelter". Many people do not like homeless shelters built in their neighborhood because they are known to lower property values. However, The Other Side Village is not a homeless shelter. At a homeless shelter, visitors come in the evening, are assigned a bed, given some food, they might be connected with some social services, and then they leave in the morning. They spend their day trying to get by another day, and then repeat the process in the evening. The homeless shelter in no way is a home to these people; it is just a temporary shelter. Therefore, although each visitor in the shelter technically has a place to sleep for that one night, they are still without a home. In contrast, the Other Side Village is a community of homes. The people who will be living in this village will not just have temporary shelter, they will have homes-homes that they take care of, take pride in, clean, manage and decorate. They will have neighbors-neighbors that they will support and that will support them. They will have to pay rent for their home. They will be expected to live by community laws, and of course the laws of the city as a whole. It is easy to jump to conclusions and assume that this village will affect home values in the surrounding neighborhood the same way a homeless shelter would, but please take a moment to consider the significant differences between these two establishments. I expect that this neighborhood will have a very small affect on home values and crime rates in the neighborhood but will definitely have larger, very positive effects on the whole city. If you are on the fence about the Other Side Village, I ask you to please seriously consider the differences between this village and a homeless shelter. Thank you. Emma Scanlon

subject: Tiny Home Village
comment: It's a complicated project on every level. I understand and empathize with residents who clearly want no part of the project. I am new. I haven't experienced the sense of abandonment and stigmatization my Westside neighbors have expressed. I, too, am discouraged by lack of investment in keeping parks safe and clean, camps by the river, broken down RVs in the neighborhood. However, I support the tiny home village. I supported it when it started, with 300 tiny homes. I saw the project succeed in Denver. I have observed housing models in Minneapolis and Duluth that have succeeded in providing stable housing to many of the most vulnerable citizens. I give our city council great praise for working hard to redesign the project to a reduced size and configuration. This is their diligent attempt to hear and respond to their constituents while supporting a much needed project. There are no easy answers to solving the social and economic problems that fuel our national crisis. The tiny Tiny Village is a start. I support it moving forward in our neighborhood. One concern is the requirement for strict sobriety. A model in Duluth allowed legal substance use in the privacy the the small studios. However, no residents were allowed only in the common space and no alcohol and drug use was allowed in these spaces. Perhaps there is a more reasonable solution for the concern about substance abuse. No one wants to be told what to do in their own home. Best wishes and thank you for your service. Deborah Esquibel Hunt, PhD
